To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the activation of mutant forms of HCA II by small molecules occurs by proton transfer between the zinc-bound solvent and exogenous proton donors/acceptors and that the binding of the small molecule to Trp-64, which lies in a region of the protein approximately 8 A away from the zinc, is responsible for the activation of the mutant.

the activation of mutant forms of HCA II occurs through the participation of exogenous proton donors in the proton transfer between the zinc-bound and solution protons, that the activation is due primarily to the interaction of these donors with a residue in the vicinity of the zinc, that this residue is Trp-64, and that the activation of the mutant is due to the binding of the donors to Trp-64 and not to the binding of these donors to the zinc.

the binding of exogenous proton donors to a mutant of human carbonic anydrase II at a site approximately 8 A removed from the zinc ion is responsible for the activation of the mutant by the exogenous proton donor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the binding of exogenous ligands to the active site of H64W and W5A-HCA II and the effects on catalysis of the binding of these ligands to the exogenous binding sites of H64W-HCA II and W5A HCA II.

a mechanism of catalysis that is not associated with a change in intrinsic catalytic ability of a protein but rather with the ability to use exogenous proton donors and acceptors to enhance catalytic ability by participation in proton transfer pathways in the active site.
the role of the proton transfer pathway in catalysis, and we have shown that activation can result from participation of exogenous proton donors/acceptors at sites other than the metal-bound water.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

proton transfer between the zinc-bound solvent and solution is a critical part of catalysis by HCA II and that small molecule rescue of the mutant enzymes occurs by a mechanism involving binding of the exogenous donor/acceptors to a site on the enzyme remote from the zinc-bound water.

the activation of W5A-HCA II by proton donors occurs by a mechanism involving binding of these proton donors to the side chain indole of Trp-65, which is approximately 8 A away from the zinc-bound water.

the proton transfer between the zinc-bound hydroxyl group and the exogenous donor occurs through a pathway that includes the indole ring and that this pathway is activated by the binding of the donor to the indole ring.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding of proton donors/acceptors to the indole ring in Trp-64 can lead to activation of the proton transfer pathway of H64W and W5A-HCA II.

small molecule rescue of mutant HCA II involves proton transfer between the active site and the exogenous donor/acceptor, and that the proton transfer occurs via the binding of the donor to the active site, followed by proton transfer to the acceptor.

proton transfer in H64W HAC II is facilitated by the binding of a donor/acceptor at Trp-64, and this is consistent with a mechanism for the rescue of mutant HCA II by small molecules in which the small molecules participate in the proton transfer between the zinc-bound solvent and solution.
The main takeaway from our work is that

small molecule rescue of mutant HCA II can be achieved by binding of exogenous proton donors to a binding site at the active site, and that this activation involves the energetics associated with proton transfer.

proton donors bound to the indole side chains of Trp-65 and Trp-64 are able to act as exogenous donors/ acceptors for the proton transfer pathway in the catalytic mechanism of HCA II, and that this is a general feature of the activation of HCA II by small molecule proton donors/acceptors.
the proton transfer pathway of HCA II, although not the primary site of binding for the exogenous donors/ acceptors, is an integral part of the catalytic mechanism.
